title: American Nathan Pare celebrated victory. Then came controversy: ‘It’s hard to deal with’
content:
LIVIGNO, Italy — These Games, they can be cruel. There was Nathan Pare, a 21-year-old snowboard cross racer, ducking his head, finding some extra speed, propelling off the final jump, and somehow, someway, overtaking two elite French riders to win his men’s snowboard cross quarterfinal heat to book his spot in the semifinals and keep his Olympic medal hopes alive.

Pare raised both hands, balled in fists, pumping away. One of the biggest races in his young career. One of the biggest wins of his young life.

U.S. coaches near the finish line leapt into the air. Pare’s family fell into a pile of hugs. Then came the official results.

Standing in front of a Milano Cortina backdrop with French racers Jonas Chollet and Loan Bozzolo, along with Spain’s Lucas Eguibar, Pare furrowed his brow, extended his arms and let out a hard, “What?”

From ecstatic to incredulous. All in about 30 seconds.

“To have a call like that, at the Olympics, pretty much stripping it away from me, it’s hard to deal with,” Pare said later, well after Austrian Alessandro Hämmerle’s mad-dash gold-medal victory.

However, not everyone agreed with Pare’s assessment. “We know, and he knows,” Eguibar said later. “I don’t know why he was complaining after the decision.”

The issue occurred on turn four.

With the two Frenchmen running first and second, Pare moved from his line (think about an imaginary line, like on a track, except on a snowboard cross course) in the middle to the left edge of the course. There, he made contact with Eguibar, sending the Spaniard spilling over, ending his chances. Sitting on the course, Eguibar was visibly upset with the contact.

“The rule is really clear,” said the 32-year-old, four-time Olympian. “If another rider is outside, you can take the line of the other guy.”

An International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) official told The Athletic the race jury automatically reviewed the run and it was determined Pare’s risky line resulted in Eguibar falling. The decision was made anonymously by all six jury members.

“There was no intentional contact, but it was a clear mistake that cut off the other athlete,” the FIS official wrote in an email. “Under the rules, if a rider makes such an error and takes another athlete out, they are ranked last in the heat. This falls under line deviation within the race interference rules.”

No protest of the decision was filed by Team USA. Still, Pare could not and would not see it any other way.

His contention — he was taking the same race line as the two riders in front of him, and it was Eguibar who went wide.

“When I started my turn, they’re saying that I deviated from my turn line to basically go into someone else’s, which I don’t necessarily feel is completely accurate,” Pare said. “If you go back and watch, I feel like the two French boys in the race, they took the exact same line as me and I followed them.

After the ruling was handed down, Pare pleaded with Vakhtang Kopadze, the race’s technical director, who was in communication with the judges. Pare was told there was nothing that could be done.

Eguibar said before the crash, on turn three, he couldn’t get to the outside line because French racers were there, so he held back and waited.

“I respect the lines,” Eguibar said. “Then in turn four, Nathan got real aggressive to the inside and really aggressive to the outside, and I was there. The rules are really clear. If you do this, and you crash with the other rider, you are out.”

While disappointed that his individual Olympic goal is over, Eguibar emphasized that this is the nature of snowboard cross. Riders take lines, contact ensues and sometimes Ranked as Last happen. He said he’s been on the other side and benefited from these falls. He said he’s accidentally caused wipeouts himself. He said Thursday he was on the wrong side of it. “These things happen,” Eguibar said.

Pare remains steadfast; he did nothing wrong. “I did everything I felt was correct,” he said. “I would probably go retake the line again if I was given the option.”

Pare said that, had he reached the semifinals, he had plenty of speed to advance through to the finals. “It’s impossible to explain how that feels,” Pare said.

While he’ll see Eguibar, Hämmerle and the rest of the top snowboard cross riders down the road in World Cup season, he’ll have to wait four years to see how far he can go in the Olympics.
